title: The Science of Imaginary Solutions: Jarry from the Mayenne to the Grave at Bagneux
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Mayenne and the Breton Coast

stops.name: Laval: born on the Mayenne
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry). The coordinate is the commemorative plaque at 15 rue Charles-Landelle, geocoded to 48.0682, -0.7728; research figures of 48.0736, -0.7699 and 48.0745, -0.766 are a generic town point and a misplaced street respectively, and are corrected here. Biographers disagree on the exact birth address.
stops.campa: A son is born in Laval, on the Mayenne, to Anselme Jarry, a merchant of cloth, and Caroline Quernest, whose people are Breton magistrates. They name him Alfred. The father's business is already thinning; the mother, who reads, and who considers trade beneath her line, keeps her own counsel in the house. Which room he was born in is still argued over, and the plaque the town fixes a century afterward names 15 rue Charles-Landelle without settling it. He is carried to the cathedral for baptism on 8 June 1874.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at 15 rue Charles-Landelle, Laval
Laval Cathedral, where he was baptized on 8 June 1874
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Laval: the household comes apart
stops.date_confidence: [R] reconstruction. Fell (2005) describes the breakdown of the household in the years before the 1879 departure but gives no date; the year here is a placeholder inside that span, and month and day are defaulted to 01. No address is attested, so the coordinate is the town centre.
stops.campa: Anselme's trade goes on failing. Caroline, unwilling to sink with a merchant who cannot hold his accounts, begins the slow work of taking her two children back toward her own family on the Breton coast. Alfred is five. He and his older sister Charlotte grow up inside a house being dismantled around them by a decision nobody announces to them. Charlotte will still be his last close tie thirty years later, in the month he dies. What the boy makes of it is not recorded, and no letter from these years survives.
suggested_refs: Fell, An Imagination in Revolt, on the separation of Anselme and Caroline Jarry
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Saint-Brieuc: nine years at the lycee
stops.date_confidence: the move to Saint-Brieuc is dated 1879 and the schooling there runs to 1888 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); no month or day is given and both are defaulted to 01. The family's address within the town is not attested, so the coordinate is town-level.
stops.campa: Caroline settles with the children in Saint-Brieuc, close to her own people, and Alfred is put into the local lycee. Teachers and classmates recall afterward a pupil given to mockery and to wordplay, carrying a private mythology into which nobody else is admitted. He learns his Latin and his Greek thoroughly, well enough to run both through his own prose later, turned against the men who taught them to him. Nine years pass here and leave almost no paper: school registers, a few remembered anecdotes, nothing in his own hand.
suggested_refs: The lycee of Saint-Brieuc, Cotes-d'Armor, attended 1879 to 1888
sources: Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

segments.name: Rennes: Pere Heb and the Theatre des Phynances

stops.name: Rennes: the physics master called Pere Heb
stops.date_confidence: entry into the rhetoric class at the Lycee de Rennes is dated October 1888 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to the Lycee Emile-Zola at 2 avenue Jean Janvier, 48.1087, -1.6750; a research figure of 48.1088, -1.6674 sits some 560 metres east of the building. Hebert's forenames Felix-Frederic and his dates, 1832 to 1917, are attested.
stops.campa: In the rhetoric class of the Lycee de Rennes stands Felix Hebert, master of physics, a heavy and ridiculed man whom successive years of pupils have already turned into a monster called Pere Heb. In their telling he is given a country to misrule, an appetite with no floor to it, and a vocabulary of his own. Jarry arrives at fifteen into a satire older than his enrollment and takes it over entirely. What detonates in a Paris theatre eight years from now is built here, in a provincial classroom, out of one exhausted teacher. Hebert dies in 1917, ten years after his pupil.
stops.quote_source: Ubu Roi (1896), Act I Scene 1, the opening word, distorting merde by one letter
suggested_refs: The Lycee Emile-Zola, formerly the Lycee de Rennes, 2 avenue Jean Janvier
sources: Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

stops.name: Rennes: the Morin brothers' attic
stops.date_confidence: the encounter is dated 1888 with no month or day, both defaulted to 01. Authorship corrected: en.wikipedia (Ubu Roi) states that Les Polonais was written by Henri Morin and his brother Charles before Jarry met it, so a research claim that Jarry co-wrote the farce is downgraded here to inheritance and adaptation. The house location within Rennes is approximate, and the name Theatre des Phynances cannot be independently dated to 1888.
stops.campa: Henri Morin and his brother Charles have already written a farce, Les Polonais, in which Pere Heb is crowned king of an imaginary Poland. Jarry inherits it. The play is not his and becomes his, and the Morins will spend decades explaining, without much success, that they wrote it first. In the Morin family's attic it is played with marionettes before an audience of classmates who call their company the Theatre des Phynances, and he feeds into it the rhythm of the dialogue and the bottomless greed of the central figure.
suggested_refs: Les Polonais, the Morin brothers' schoolboy farce, ancestor of Ubu Roi
sources: Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

segments.name: Paris: the Student Who Never Enters the Ecole

stops.name: Paris: Bergson's classroom at the Lycee Henri-IV
stops.date_confidence: the year 1891 is attested (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01. Two research coordinates for the lycee differ, 48.8462, 2.3468 and 48.8462, 2.3488; the western figure is kept here and the discrepancy of some 150 metres is left standing rather than silently averaged.
stops.campa: He passes the second part of his baccalaureat with distinction and comes to Paris to prepare the entrance examination of the Ecole Normale Superieure. At the Lycee Henri-IV, behind the Pantheon, philosophy is taught by Henri Bergson, whose lectures on duration and on laughter he takes down and keeps. Leon-Paul Fargue and Albert Thibaudet are in the same classes. The provincial boy is now inside the apparatus that produces the Republic's professors, and he is taking notes from the seat of a pupil. Bergson's courses here run from 1891 to 1893.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Henri-IV, rue Clovis, and Bergson's courses of 1891 to 1893
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Paris: the Latin Quarter rooms and three refusals
stops.date_confidence: corrected. fr.wikipedia states he failed the Ecole Normale Superieure entrance three times in succession, plus two unsuccessful attempts at the licence; a research claim of two failures in 1893 and 1894 is wrong on the count and unsupported on the years. No examination venue can be pinned, so the coordinate is the Pantheon and rue Cujas quarter where he lodged, and the year is a placeholder inside the run of attempts.
stops.campa: He rooms in the streets around the Pantheon, minutes from the lycee and from the cafes where the symbolist generation argues nightly. Three times he sits the entrance examination of the Ecole Normale Superieure, and three times it refuses him; two attempts at the licence fail as well. The career his mother wanted for him closes. He does not appear to grieve it. He is already writing and already publishing in the little reviews. In which years he sat the examination, and in what room, no source reached will say.
suggested_refs: The Ecole Normale Superieure, rue d'Ulm, which refused him three times
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Paris: two prizes at L'Echo de Paris
stops.date_confidence: the two prose competitions are dated to May and July 1893 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the stop is dated to the year with month and day defaulted to 01, since it carries both. The canonical Paris pin is inherited unchanged from the existing atlas files.
stops.campa: Twice in one year the newspaper L'Echo de Paris gives him a prose prize, in May and again in July, and pays him two hundred and fifty gold francs for the pair. They are his first published texts, and the Ubu figure is already inside them, brought whole from a Rennes attic into the Paris press. He is twenty years old and holds no diploma; the first money writing has ever earned him was paid for the schoolboy monster. In December he joins the staff of the little magazine L'Art litteraire.
suggested_refs: L'Echo de Paris, prize texts of May and July 1893
L'Art litteraire, joined December 1893

stops.name: Paris: the influenza, and his mother
stops.date_confidence: [R]. en.wikipedia (Alfred Jarry) reports that Jarry caught influenza and that Caroline fell ill nursing him and died of it; fr.wikipedia corroborates the death in 1893 without the sequence. The place is contested: Fell (2005) and Arnaud (1974) disagree on whether she died in Paris or in Laval, and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved. Month and day are not attested and are defaulted.
stops.campa: He falls ill with influenza. His mother nurses him, catches it, and dies of it; that is the account that has come down. Caroline Quernest had left a failing husband, moved her children twice, and pushed her son toward the Ecole that refused him three times. She does not live to see the play. Her death leaves him a small inheritance, which steadies his finances for a season. Where she died the sources will not settle: some biographers put it in Paris, over the sickbed, and others back in Laval.
suggested_refs: Fell (2005) and Arnaud (1974), contradicting each other on the place of Caroline Quernest's death
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)
Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

segments.name: Pont-Aven, the Mercure, and the Barracks

stops.name: Pont-Aven: the Pension Gloanec
stops.date_confidence: May 1894 is attested (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He takes a room at the Pension Gloanec in Pont-Aven, where the painters eat cheaply and argue about flatness and outline, and there he meets Paul Gauguin, Armand Seguin, Charles Filiger and the Irishman Roderic O'Conor. What he takes from the Pont-Aven circle is not a subject but a method: the black line, the wood block, the refusal of modelling. He is cutting his own engravings by now. Ten of them will go into the book he publishes in October, printed from blocks he cut himself.
suggested_refs: The Pension Gloanec, Pont-Aven, and the painters of the Pont-Aven circle
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Paris: reading Ubu at the Mercure de France
stops.date_confidence: the reading at the home of Alfred Vallette and Rachilde is dated 1894 without month; the publication of Les Minutes de sable memorial is dated October 1894 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry). The stop carries both and takes the attested month, with the day defaulted to 01. The Mercure de France address is area-level.
stops.campa: At the house of Alfred Vallette and his wife Rachilde, who run the Mercure de France, Jarry reads an early Ubu aloud to a room of writers. Rachilde will still be describing that voice thirty years later, flat and metallic, hammering each syllable as though the words were being counted out on a table. The Mercure takes him in, and the couple become the fixed point he returns to for the rest of his life. In October it prints Les Minutes de sable memorial, poems and prose set with ten of his own wood engravings.
suggested_refs: Les Minutes de sable memorial (Mercure de France, October 1894), with ten wood engravings by the author
sources: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928)
Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

stops.name: Paris: L'Ymagier, with Remy de Gourmont
stops.date_confidence: the founding of L'Ymagier is dated 1894 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01. The office address is not confirmed, so the coordinate is area-level.
stops.campa: With Remy de Gourmont he founds and co-edits L'Ymagier, a quarterly given over to woodcuts, devotional prints, playing cards, Epinal images: the popular visual traditions the symbolists collect and the academies ignore. Jarry sets his own engravings beside anonymous fifteenth-century blocks without a word of apology for the company, and writes the notes that place them there. The partnership sours inside two years and he leaves it, taking nothing but the printing debts. The taste does not leave him; he is still cutting his own blocks for his own books a decade later.
stops.quote: The work of art, by definition, is a stuffed crocodile.
stops.quote_source: Alfred Jarry, Selected Works, ed. Roger Shattuck and Simon Watson Taylor (Jonathan Cape, London, 1965)
suggested_refs: L'Ymagier, the quarterly of popular imagery co-edited with Remy de Gourmont, 1894 to 1896

stops.name: Laval: the 101st Infantry Regiment
stops.date_confidence: corrected, and the two research lenses contradict each other. One gives the 149th Infantry Regiment, an Epinal unit; the other, followed here, gives the 101st, which had been garrisoned at Laval since 1877 (fr.wikipedia, 101e regiment d'infanterie). Conscription is dated 1894 with no month or day, both defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Conscription puts him in uniform in the town he was born in, at the barracks of the 101st Infantry. He is very small and very thin, and no issue tunic in the depot comes near fitting him; the regiment makes a running joke of the sight of him under a greatcoat cut for a farm boy. He drills, is inspected, and is marched about the Mayenne in clothes that swallow him. The unit is disputed: one account gives the 149th, an Epinal regiment, against the 101st that had garrisoned Laval since 1877.
suggested_refs: The barracks of the 101st Infantry Regiment at Laval
sources: Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

stops.name: Laval: his father dies, and the army releases him
stops.date_confidence: both the death of Anselme Jarry and the medical discharge are dated 1895 (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); no month or day is given for either and both are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Anselme Jarry dies, and his son inherits a small sum which he spends fast on books and on printing. In the same year the army discharges him as unfit, the papers naming chronic biliary lithiasis. He is twenty-two, orphaned of both parents inside two years, released from the barracks and from any expectation anyone still had of him. That year he publishes Cesar-Antechrist, and Pere Ubu walks into print in it, out of the schoolroom at last. Neither the death nor the discharge is dated in the record beyond the year.
suggested_refs: Cesar-Antechrist (1895), the first substantial appearance of Pere Ubu in print

stops.name: Paris: the Clement Luxe bicycle
stops.date_confidence: the purchase is dated 1896 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01. The canonical Paris pin is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: He buys a Clement Luxe racing bicycle from a merchant named Trochon and never finishes paying for it. Trochon's bills follow him from address to address for years. He will build a whole novel around a man who out-pedals a locomotive, and he never settles the account for the machine he rode while writing it. The public figure is built on it too: the small man in cyclist's shoes and a woman's blouse, riding Paris at speed with a revolver in his pocket, arriving at literary evenings with his trousers still clipped.
suggested_refs: The Clement Luxe bicycle bought from Trochon and never paid for

stops.name: Paris: Ubu roi in print
stops.date_confidence: corrected to month precision. fr.wikipedia gives only June 1896 for the Mercure de France book edition, so a research date of 10 June 1896 is not supported and the day is defaulted to 01. The fr.wikipedia article on Ubu roi records an earlier printing in Paul Fort's Le Livre d'art on 25 April 1896.
stops.campa: The Mercure de France publishes Ubu roi as a book, two months after Paul Fort has printed it in Le Livre d'art. The text that leaves the press is a schoolboy lampoon of a physics teacher, grown into five acts about a coward who murders a king, taxes a country to death, and flees by ship when the country tires of him. In the stage directions Poland is nowhere. Fort's printing is dated to the twenty-fifth of April; the Mercure's carries no date more precise than June.
stops.quote: S'il n'y avait pas de Pologne il n'y aurait pas de Polonais !
stops.quote_source: Ubu Roi (1896), the closing line of Act V, spoken by Pere Ubu
suggested_refs: Ubu roi, Mercure de France book edition, June 1896

stops.name: Nouveau-Theatre: the speech before the curtain
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The venue is the Nouveau-Theatre, 15 rue Blanche in the 9th arrondissement, used by Lugne-Poe's Theatre de l'Oeuvre (en.wikipedia, Ubu Roi). Three research lenses gave three different coordinates for the same building, 48.8746/2.3316, 48.8811/2.3305 and 48.8802/2.3287; all are corrected and unified on 48.8786, 2.3314, from the fr.wikipedia entry for the Theatre de Paris at that address.
stops.campa: Aurelien Lugne-Poe has taken the play for the Theatre de l'Oeuvre and hired the Nouveau-Theatre in the rue Blanche for it. Firmin Gemier will play Ubu in a pear-shaped costume with a spiral on the belly, the sets are painted flat by a committee of painters, and a single actor in a placard walks on to announce the changes of scene. Before the curtain Jarry comes out in front of the house and, in that hammering voice, tells the audience exactly how little they are obliged to read into what they are about to watch.
stops.quote: You are free to see in M. Ubu however many allusions you care to, or else a simple puppet, a school boy's caricature of one of his teachers who personified for him all the ugliness in the world
stops.quote_source: Jarry's curtain speech before the premiere of Ubu Roi, Nouveau-Theatre, Paris, 10 December 1896, as quoted in en.wikipedia, Ubu Roi
suggested_refs: The Nouveau-Theatre, 15 rue Blanche, Paris 9e, now the Theatre de Paris

stops.name: Nouveau-Theatre: the riot
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the coordinate is the unified figure explained at the previous stop. The commonly repeated figure of roughly fifteen minutes of uproar is not carried by either fr.wikipedia or en.wikipedia, which record only that a riot broke out, and it is demoted here from attested to unverified.
stops.campa: Gemier steps forward and says the first word, one letter longer than the obscenity it comes from, and the house comes apart. Partisans and enemies shout each other down; the play goes on being fought over rather than watched. In the audience sits William Butler Yeats, who has come from Dublin and London and follows almost none of the French, and who understands well enough what has been done to the theatre he was raised on. He goes back that night to the Hotel Corneille and writes down what he thinks is now coming.
stops.quote: Feeling bound to support the most spirited party, we have shouted for the play, but that night at the Hotel Corneille I am very sad, for comedy, objectivity, has displayed its growing power once more. I say, 'After Stephane Mallarme, after Paul Verlaine, after Gustave Moreau, after Puvis de Chavannes, after our own verse, after all our subtle colour and nervous rhythm, after the faint mixed tints of Conder, what more is possible? After us the Savage God.'
stops.quote_source: W. B. Yeats, The Trembling of the Veil (1922), recalling the premiere of Ubu Roi
suggested_refs: Yeats, The Trembling of the Veil (1922), on the night of 10 December 1896
Contemporary Paris press accounts of the premiere, December 1896
sources: W. B. Yeats, The Trembling of the Veil (1922)

stops.name: Paris: the Theatre des Pantins
stops.date_confidence: the puppet Ubu roi at the Theatre des Pantins is dated 20 January 1898 (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry). Coordinate corrected: the theatre was at 6 rue Ballu in the 9th arrondissement, which geocodes to 48.8819, 2.3300; a research figure of 48.8837, 2.3186 lands nearly a kilometre west, by the place de Clichy.
stops.campa: In Claude Terrasse's own studio at 6 rue Ballu, in the ninth arrondissement, Jarry, Terrasse and Franc-Nohain fit out a marionette theatre for adults and call it the Theatre des Pantins. Pierre Bonnard designs the sets and the costumes; Terrasse writes the music. On 20 January 1898 Ubu roi is played there by puppets, fourteen months after the scandal at the Nouveau-Theatre shut most other doors to it. The play has gone back to the strings it was born on in a Rennes attic, in a room lent by the man who scored it.
suggested_refs: The Theatre des Pantins, 6 rue Ballu, Paris 9e, with sets and costumes by Pierre Bonnard

stops.name: Paris: Oscar Wilde comes to see him
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is dated May 1898 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01. No location within Paris is attested, so the canonical Paris pin is used.
stops.campa: Oscar Wilde, a year out of Reading Gaol and living in Paris under the name Sebastian Melmoth, meets the author of Ubu roi. He is broke, cut by most of the English he passes in the street, and drinking in the cafes of the rue de Rivoli on money sent by the few friends who stayed. Jarry is twenty-five and famous for one riot. One of them was destroyed by a scandal he did not choose; the other manufactured his own and is living off it. Wilde has eighteen months left, Jarry nine years. What they said to each other that spring is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: Wilde's Paris exile of 1897 to 1900, under the name Sebastian Melmoth

stops.name: Alfortville: the mahogany skiff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry). Coordinate corrected: the research figure of 48.6333, 2.4333 falls in open country near Etiolles and matches neither named place; the purchase was made at Alfortville, which geocodes to 48.8052, 2.4197. Corbeil-Essonnes, where the boat was overhauled, is 48.6136, 2.4820.
stops.campa: On the ninth of July he buys a mahogany skiff at Alfortville and names it L'As, the Ace. He hauls it upriver to the house Vallette and Rachilde keep on the Seine and refits it there with Vallette, the two of them scraping and varnishing at the water's edge. From now on his Paris is joined to the river by muscle: he rows down to Corbeil, fishes, rows back, and writes on the bank. The bicycle and the skiff are the only two machines he owns. The boat is overhauled downstream at Corbeil-Essonnes, where he will later buy his one piece of ground.
suggested_refs: L'As, the mahogany skiff bought at Alfortville on 9 July 1897

stops.name: Paris: the Grande Chasubliere, 7 rue Cassette
stops.date_confidence: the move is dated November 1897, to the deuxieme etage et demi at 7 rue Cassette (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to 48.8505, 2.3309 for that address; a research figure of 48.8496, 2.3288 sits about 180 metres off. A rival claim placing this room on the boulevard de Port-Royal is superseded: Port-Royal is the lodging he was evicted from.
stops.campa: Evicted from the boulevard de Port-Royal, he takes a room at 7 rue Cassette that a landlord has made by cutting one storey into two. It is some twenty-five square metres and the ceiling stops short of his full height, which is not great. Visitors stoop to come in and stay stooping. Above and below him the building houses religious publishers and dealers in vestments, so he names the place the Grande Chasubliere. He lives there, on and off, for the last ten years of his life.
suggested_refs: 7 rue Cassette, Paris 6e, the half-storey room he called the Grande Chasubliere
sources: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928)

stops.name: Paris: Doctor Faustroll is drafted
stops.date_confidence: the drafting of Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien is dated 1897 in one lens and 1898 in the standard accounts of composition; the year 1897 is kept with month and day defaulted to 01. The book was not published until 1911. No writing address is attested for the drafting, so the canonical Paris pin is used.
stops.campa: He writes a novel in which a doctor named Faustroll, born at sixty-three years of age, sails a copper sieve across the streets of Paris as though they were water, accompanied by a bailiff and a baboon. Inside it he sets out the science the book exists to found. It is a joke conducted with the full apparatus of proof: definitions, theorems, dedications to living painters and writers. The manuscript goes into a drawer. The drafting runs across 1897 and 1898, and nothing of the book is printed while he is alive.
stops.quote: 'Pataphysics is the science of that which is superinduced upon metaphysics, whether within or beyond the latter's limitations, extending as far beyond metaphysics as the latter extends beyond physics.
stops.quote_source: Exploits and Opinions of Dr. Faustroll, Pataphysician (written 1898, published 1911), as quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Pataphysics; translator not identified on the page
suggested_refs: Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien, drafted 1897 to 1898

stops.name: Le Coudray-Montceaux: the Phalanstere and the revolver
stops.date_confidence: the riverside years run roughly 1898 to 1906; the year here opens that span and month and day are defaulted to 01. The pistol anecdote is dated 1901 by one lens and is [R]: it comes to us through Rachilde (1928) and is repeated in every later biography, with the wording varying between tellings. en.wikipedia carries a different English rendering of the same reply.
stops.campa: Below Corbeil, near the riverside house Vallette and Rachilde call the Phalanstere, Jarry rents a hut on the bank and lives in it for stretches of the next eight years. He fishes, rows, drinks what he can afford, and fires a revolver at the trees in the garden. A neighbour comes over the fence to complain that the shooting is a danger to her children. What he answers her becomes the most repeated sentence of his life, and no two accounts of it agree word for word.
stops.quote: Si l'un de vos enfants avait ete tue, nous vous en aurions fait d'autres.
stops.quote_source: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928); accents removed. en.wikipedia gives the English variant 'If that should ever happen, ma-da-me, we should ourselves be happy to get new ones with you.'
suggested_refs: The Phalanstere, the Vallette and Rachilde house on the Seine below Corbeil
sources: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928)
Noel Arnaud, Alfred Jarry, d'Ubu roi au docteur Faustroll (1974)

stops.name: Paris: rue Laffitte, Vollard and La Revue blanche
stops.date_confidence: corrected. fr.wikipedia records that La Revue blanche published Jarry from May 1896 to April 1903, so the association is a seven-year span and not a 1901 event; the research description of him as a kind of secretary to the Natanson brothers is not attested in any source reached and is downgraded. The year 1901 is kept as a point inside the span, with month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The rue Laffitte holds two of the addresses that keep him alive. Ambroise Vollard, who deals in Cezanne and prints illustrated books, commissions work from him. The Natanson brothers' Revue blanche prints him steadily from 1896 to 1903, in the company of Toulouse-Lautrec's lithographs and Mallarme's late prose. The money is irregular and small and it is what he has. He writes almanacs, chronicles, speculative columns, whatever the reviews will take.
stops.quote: Cliches are the armature of the Absolute.
stops.quote_source: Alfred Jarry, Selected Works, ed. Roger Shattuck and Simon Watson Taylor (Jonathan Cape, London, 1965)
suggested_refs: La Revue blanche, which published Jarry from May 1896 to April 1903
Ambroise Vollard's gallery and press, rue Laffitte
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Paris: Henri Rousseau's studio in Plaisance
stops.date_confidence: the friendship is dated to roughly 1900 to 1906 by Shattuck, The Banquet Years (1955); the year here sits inside that span and month and day are defaulted to 01. The studio address within the Plaisance quarter is approximate.
stops.campa: In a poor quarter south of Montparnasse a retired customs official paints jungles he has never seen, and Jarry, who was born in the same town in the Mayenne as Henri Rousseau, climbs the stairs to look at them. He praises the canvases in print when almost nobody else will, and Rousseau paints his portrait. The picture is later damaged and cut down until almost nothing of the sitter remains. How that happened, and who did it, the accounts do not agree on. Apollinaire and Picasso find their way to this studio in the next few years.
suggested_refs: Rousseau's lost portrait of Jarry
Shattuck, The Banquet Years (1955), on the Rousseau circle
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Paris: Ubu enchaine
stops.date_confidence: Ubu enchaine is dated 1900 and L'Amour absolu 1899 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); no months or days are given and both are defaulted. The canonical Paris pin is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: A year after the novel L'Amour absolu he publishes a sequel to the play that made him. In it Ubu, no longer a king, becomes obsessed with liberty and pursues it by enslaving himself, in a country where the free are compelled by law to be free. The comedy of the first play was appetite. The comedy of this one is the word freedom, spoken by a man volunteering for the galleys and demanding, as his right, to be chained. He writes it in the years when his own liberty consists of a rented half-storey, an unpaid bicycle and a hut on the Seine. It goes out as a printed text; no theatre stages it while he lives.
stops.quote: We shall not have succeeded in demolishing everything unless we demolish the ruins as well. But the only way I can see of doing that is to use them to put up a lot of fine, well-designed buildings.
stops.quote_source: Alfred Jarry, Ubu enchaine (1900), the epigraph standing before Act I, spoken by Pere Ubu; French text verified on fr.wikisource
suggested_refs: Ubu enchaine (1900)
L'Amour absolu (1899)

stops.name: Corbeil: writing Le Surmale
stops.date_confidence: Le Surmale is published in 1902 and Messaline in 1901 (fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); months and days are not given and are defaulted. The writing is placed between the riverside hut and the rue Cassette room from the known residences of those years, which is reconstruction rather than record.
stops.campa: Between the hut on the Seine and the half-storey in the rue Cassette he writes Le Surmale, in which a man beats a locomotive over ten thousand miles on a bicycle, running on a chemical food, and afterward performs an act of love eighty-two times in a day, and is killed at last by a machine built to make him love it back. He is writing about engines and appetite while living on almost nothing. Messaline, a Roman novel of an empress who cannot be satisfied, had gone out the year before.
suggested_refs: Le Surmale (1902)
Messaline (1901)
sources: Jill Fell, Alfred Jarry: An Imagination in Revolt (2005)

stops.name: Le Grand-Lemps: La Dragonne begun
stops.date_confidence: the stay with Claude Terrasse at Le Grand-Lemps and the beginning of La Dragonne are dated 1904 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected to 45.3992, 5.4206, the commune's own figure; the research value of 45.4667, 5.5833 sits some fourteen kilometres off.
stops.campa: He goes south to the Isere, to the house of Claude Terrasse, who wrote the music for the puppet Ubu and who married into money. Fed and housed for a while, out of Paris and out of debt collectors' reach, he starts a novel called La Dragonne, about a soldier and a war. He works at it for the last three years of his life and never finishes it. What exists of it is assembled after his death by his sister Charlotte and by Jean Saltas, the doctor who befriended him in 1897.
suggested_refs: La Dragonne, unfinished, begun at Le Grand-Lemps in 1904

stops.name: Corbeil: the Tripode
stops.date_confidence: corrected. fr.wikipedia places the acquisition of the small Corbeil property and the order for the cabin at the end of 1904, with an enlargement of the holding in July 1905, so a research date of 1905 is slightly late. The day is defaulted to 01. Coordinate is Corbeil-Essonnes at 48.6136, 2.4820.
stops.campa: With no money he buys a strip of land near Corbeil at the end of 1904 and orders a wooden cabin for it at once, a shed on legs he calls the Tripode. It is the only property he ever owns. He enlarges the plot the following July, borrowing against nothing, and plans a garden on it. The cabin is a rudimentary thing, made by a carpenter and stood on legs above the damp ground. He is thirty-one. Within eighteen months the creditors take the whole of it back off him.
suggested_refs: The Tripode, the cabin built on Jarry's plot near Corbeil at the end of 1904

stops.name: Laval: the fever and the last rites
stops.date_confidence: the letter to Rachilde is dated 28 May 1906 and the delirious fever, the last rites and the writing of his own will are dated to May 1906 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry). The refuge with his sister Charlotte is [R], drawn from the same article's account of his correspondence. The coordinate is town-level, since Charlotte's address in Laval is not attested.
stops.campa: He goes back to Laval, to his sister, in the state his friends have been watching approach for a year. He writes to Rachilde from there, on the twenty-eighth of May, describing himself as a machine running down, an engine whose parts are giving out one after another. That month the fever takes him into delirium; a priest is called and gives him the last rites; between crises he writes out his own will in his own hand. Then he does not die. He gets up and lives another eighteen months.
suggested_refs: Jarry's letters to Rachilde of May 1906, from Laval
sources: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928)

stops.name: Corbeil: the land sold to the creditors
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia confirms the sale of the Corbeil land in June 1906 to appease creditors but names neither a buyer nor an intermediary; the research claims that his sister Charlotte bought it and that Octave Mirbeau and Thadee Natanson arranged the money are unattested and are not carried here. The day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The strip of land goes, eighteen months after he bought it, to pay what he owes. Who buys it, and who arranged the transaction, the record does not say; the names that circulate in the biographies are not in any document reached. The Tripode stands on somebody else's ground now, and he goes on using it as though it were his, rowing down and sleeping there when Paris turns him out. There is nothing else left to sell except paper. He keeps the room in the rue Cassette, where the ceiling is too low to stand up under.
suggested_refs: The June 1906 sale of the Corbeil plot

stops.name: Laval: the last photograph
stops.date_confidence: the photograph is dated July 1906 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01. The place within Laval is not specified, so the coordinate is town-level.
stops.campa: The last known photograph of him is taken at Laval that summer: Jarry fencing with Felix Blaviel, both men in white, masks on, blades up, the smaller figure holding his guard. It is two months since a priest stood over him with the oils. He is thirty-two in the picture, has sixteen months left, and weighs, by every account of these years, almost nothing. There is no later image of him. What the plate holds is a man on guard in the sun with a sword in his hand.
suggested_refs: The July 1906 photograph of Jarry fencing with Felix Blaviel at Laval

stops.name: Paris: the Closerie des Lilas
stops.date_confidence: attendance at Paul Fort's Vers et prose evenings at the Closerie des Lilas is dated 1906 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Paul Fort holds his Vers et prose evenings at the Closerie des Lilas, where the boulevard du Montparnasse meets the boulevard Saint-Michel, and Jarry comes to them through 1906, in what is left of his health. It is a walk from the room in the rue Cassette. The room is full of men fifteen years younger than he is, Guillaume Apollinaire among them, who have read Ubu roi as schoolboys and treat its author as an institution. They buy him drinks. He is thirty-three.
suggested_refs: The Vers et prose evenings at the Closerie des Lilas, organized by Paul Fort

stops.name: Paris: the manuscripts sold to Lemasle
stops.date_confidence: the sale of manuscripts to the autograph dealer Victor Lemasle and the publication of the memoir of Albert Samain are both dated April 1907 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is defaulted to 01. The canonical Paris pin is used, since no address is attested.
stops.campa: He sells most of the manuscripts he still holds to Victor Lemasle, a dealer in autographs, for whatever they raise. In the same month he publishes his last book, a short memoir of the poet Albert Samain, dead some years and remembered here by a man with seven months to live. His own papers go by the sheet to a trader in the handwriting of the dead, and the last thing he sets in print is a commemoration written for somebody else. What Lemasle paid for them is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Albert Samain (souvenirs), Jarry's last published book, April 1907

stops.name: Paris: found in the Chasubliere
stops.date_confidence: the discovery of Jarry in advanced physical collapse at the rue Cassette room and his removal to hospital are dated October 1907 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); the day is not given and is defaulted to 01. The coordinate is 7 rue Cassette, as corrected earlier in this file.
stops.campa: Friends who have not seen him for weeks force the door of the half-storey and find him on the floor, unable to stand, in a room stripped of nearly everything that could be sold. For years he has drunk absinthe and, when there was no money for drink, ether, calling alcohol by a name of his own. They carry him down the narrow stairs and take him across to the Hopital de la Charite in the rue Jacob, a few streets away. He does not come back to the room.
stops.quote_source: Jarry's own term for alcohol, as quoted in en.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry, where the passage carries no footnote; the companion phrase for absinthe, 'green goddess', appears in the same unsourced sentence
suggested_refs: 7 rue Cassette, the Grande Chasubliere, October 1907

stops.name: Paris: the Hopital de la Charite
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the hour: 1 November 1907 at 4.15 in the afternoon, at the Hopital de la Charite, 47 rue Jacob in the 6th arrondissement, of tuberculous meningitis (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry; en.wikipedia for the cause). Coordinate corrected to 48.8554, 2.3316, the hospital site at 45 rue des Saints-Peres and 47 rue Jacob; a research figure of 48.8534, 2.3339 sits some 290 metres southeast. The toothpick is [R]: the anecdote is repeated by every biographer and by both Wikipedias, where it carries no citation; a claimed footnote to Mark Ford in the New York Review of Books was checked and does not mention it.
stops.campa: He dies at a quarter past four in the afternoon of the first of November, of tuberculous meningitis, worsened by years of drink and hunger and ether. He is thirty-four years old. Rachilde is at the hospital, and it is her account of the afternoon that the century will keep. The story repeated ever since, by everyone who wrote about him and on the authority of no document anybody has produced, is that he was asked what he wanted, that he answered a toothpick, and that somebody in the ward went and found one and put it in his hand.
stops.quote_source: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928), reporting his last request; accents removed. The anecdote is uncited in both Wikipedias and no primary source for it was located
suggested_refs: The Hopital de la Charite, 47 rue Jacob and 45 rue des Saints-Peres, Paris 6e
sources: Rachilde, Alfred Jarry ou le Surmale des lettres (1928)

stops.name: Bagneux: the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial is dated November 1907 without a day, which is defaulted to 01 and is therefore not the true date of the funeral. Coordinate corrected to 48.8056, 2.3083, the Cimetiere parisien de Bagneux at 45 avenue Marx-Dormoy; two research figures, 48.7947/2.3131 and 48.7936/2.3121, sit over a kilometre south in the town itself. fr.wikipedia names the mourners as Vallette, Rachilde, Mirbeau, Valery and Leautaud; a research claim adding Apollinaire and Leon-Paul Fargue is unattested and is not carried.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Cimetiere parisien de Bagneux, south of Paris, in the twenty-third division, fifth row, fifth plot. Alfred Vallette and Rachilde are there, who took him in at twenty-one and buried him at thirty-four; Octave Mirbeau; Paul Valery; Paul Leautaud. It is a small group for a man whose name half of literary Paris could pronounce. The Paris press that jeered the play eleven years earlier reports the funeral. His sister Charlotte, in Laval, is the only family left, and what she inherits is an unfinished novel and a bundle of unpaid bills. No source reached records the day.
suggested_refs: The Cimetiere parisien de Bagneux, 23rd division, 5th row, 5th plot

stops.name: Paris: Picasso takes the revolver
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia (Alfred Jarry) records that Picasso acquired Jarry's revolver after his death, later collected a number of his manuscripts, and drew his portrait, but gives no date for any of the three. The year here is a placeholder immediately after the death and carries no attestation; month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: The revolver Jarry carried in his pocket and fired into the trees at Le Coudray-Montceaux passes, after his death, to Pablo Picasso, who keeps it. He had carried it for years, on the bicycle and at literary evenings, and had once answered a neighbour's complaint about the shooting. Picasso goes on to collect a number of the manuscripts as they surface on the market, and draws the dead man's portrait. When any of the three happened, no source reached will say. Within two years the painters of the rue Ravignan are building an art out of dismantled objects, and one of them has the pistol in a drawer.
suggested_refs: Picasso's acquisition of Jarry's revolver and manuscripts

stops.name: Paris: Faustroll printed at last
stops.date_confidence: the posthumous publication by Fasquelle is dated 1911 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01. The quotation carried here was verified against the French text on fr.wikisource, Livre VIII, De la surface de Dieu, where it stands as the penultimate sentence of the book; a research note calling it unsourced is corrected.
stops.campa: Four years after his death, Fasquelle publishes Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien, the book he drafted in the half-storey and never saw printed. The definition it contains, of a science of imaginary solutions that attributes to objects the properties of their virtuality, now exists in a form that can be cited and argued with. The last proposition of the book before that definition is a line of geometry about God. Faustroll speaks it, not Jarry.
stops.quote: God is the tangential point between zero and infinity.
stops.quote_source: Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien, Book VIII, De la surface de Dieu (written 1898, published 1911); French text verified on fr.wikisource, English in the Shattuck and Watson Taylor translation tradition
suggested_refs: Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien (Fasquelle, 1911)
sources: fr.wikisource, Gestes et opinions du docteur Faustroll, pataphysicien

stops.name: Paris: the Theatre Alfred Jarry
stops.date_confidence: the founding of the Theatre Alfred Jarry by Antonin Artaud, Roger Vitrac and Robert Aron at the Theatre de Grenelle is dated 1926, and the Strindberg evening at which Andre Breton was barred is dated June 1928 (artaud.journey.json). Month and day are defaulted to 01. The canonical Paris pin is inherited unchanged rather than pinned to the Grenelle house.
stops.campa: Nineteen years after the funeral, Antonin Artaud, with Roger Vitrac and Robert Aron, opens a theatre in Paris and names it for the father of Ubu. Artaud had been given his own first stage role by Lugne-Poe, who launched Ubu roi on the world. In June 1928 the company plays Strindberg's Dream Play; the surrealists come to wreck the evening, Artaud denounces his own patrons from the stage, police cordon the second night, and Andre Breton is turned away at the door of a house carrying Jarry's name.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Alfred Jarry, founded 1926 at the Theatre de Grenelle by Artaud, Vitrac and Aron

stops.name: Paris: the College de 'Pataphysique
stops.date_confidence: the founding is dated 1948 (en.wikipedia, College de 'Pataphysique); month and day are defaulted to 01. No founding-meeting address was confirmed, so the canonical Paris pin is used. The claimed lineage from the College to the Situationist International around Guy Debord is [R] and contested: Asger Jorn belonged to both, but no direct textual link between Jarry and the Debord file exists, and the atlas queue itself flags the connection as inference.
stops.campa: A group of admirers in Paris, Emmanuel Peillet among them, constitutes the College de 'Pataphysique as a body for learned and inutilious research, under the motto Eadem mutata resurgo, I arise again the same though changed. It has satraps, a calendar of its own, and honorary members. Twelve years later the Oulipo begins inside it as a subcommittee, with Raymond Queneau among its founders. The College suspends public activity from 1975 to 2000 and calls the interval its occultation.
stops.quote: 'Pataphysics will be, above all, the science of the particular... will examine the laws governing exceptions, and will explain the universe supplementary to this one.
stops.quote_source: Exploits and Opinions of Dr. Faustroll, Pataphysician, as quoted in en.wikipedia, 'Pataphysics; the ellipsis is present in the source page and the translator is not identified
suggested_refs: The College de 'Pataphysique, founded Paris 1948
The Oulipo, begun as a subcommittee of the College

stops.name: Laval: Zadkine's bronze
stops.date_confidence: the inauguration of Ossip Zadkine's bronze on the esplanade des droits de l'homme at Laval is dated 1966 (fr.wikipedia, Alfred Jarry); month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The town that could not agree which house he was born in puts up a bronze of him by Ossip Zadkine, on the esplanade des droits de l'homme, fifty-nine years after his death. It is the same town where his father's shop failed and where the 101st Infantry could not find a tunic to fit him. Six years later Gallimard begins issuing his collected works in the Bibliotheque de la Pleiade, in three volumes on India paper. Between 2012 and 2022 Classiques Garnier produces a six-volume critical edition.
suggested_refs: Ossip Zadkine's Alfred Jarry, esplanade des droits de l'homme, Laval, 1966
The Gallimard Pleiade edition of the Oeuvres completes, from 1972

stops.name: Bagneux: the concession never renewed
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources. fr.wikipedia, citing cemetery documentation, records that the burial concession was never renewed and that the remains were nevertheless not exhumed; no year is given for the lapse, and the date here is a placeholder with no attestation. Popular accounts describing the tomb as lost outright and its occupant swept into a common grave contradict that documentation, and the contradiction is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: The concession on the plot at Bagneux is never renewed. By the ordinary rule of the cemetery the ground should have been cleared and reused, and it was not: the documentation records that the remains stay where they were put, in the twenty-third division, under a stone nobody maintains. Popular accounts say the tomb was lost and the body tipped into a common grave. The papers say otherwise. No year is recorded for the lapse, and both stories are still in circulation.
suggested_refs: The unrenewed concession at the Cimetiere parisien de Bagneux, 23rd division
